b: First and Second Chronicles are another pair that began as one book, with sixty-five chapters in all. They retell the story from Adam to the return from Babylon, but with a different aim from Samuel and Kings. In the Hebrew Bible they come last of all, and the Hebrew title means "the events of the days."

The author is unnamed, though Jewish tradition says Ezra. The closing verses refer to the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC, so the book was written after the return, probably in the fifth or fourth century BC. It was meant for a small, discouraged community living under Persian rule in a rebuilt Jerusalem.
## How it is arranged

- 1 Chronicles 1 to 9: family trees from Adam to those who returned from exile.
- 1 Chronicles 10 to 29: the reign of David, with the ark, the temple plans and his last charge to Solomon.
- 2 Chronicles 1 to 9: Solomon and the temple.
- 2 Chronicles 10 to 36: the kings of Judah, ending with the fall of Jerusalem and Cyrus's decree.
## What to look for

Chronicles focuses on temple worship, the line of David and the people's identity. It leaves out David's sin with Bathsheba and concentrates on the promises. The message to the returned exiles is that they are still the people of the promise, that worship in the temple still matters, and that God answers when his people humble themselves and seek him (2 Chronicles 7:14). The last words of the Hebrew Bible are an invitation to go up to Jerusalem.

First Corinthians has sixteen chapters and is Paul's answer to a church that had a lot of problems. Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port, known for its immorality, and the believers there had absorbed many of the habits of the city. The letter is a model of how to deal with them.

Paul planted the church in about AD 50 to 51 on his second journey (Acts 18) and wrote this letter from Ephesus, about AD 53 to 55. He was responding both to a report he had heard and to a list of questions that the church had sent him. He refers to an earlier letter that has not survived (5:9).
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 4: divisions in the church, and the contrast between the wisdom of the world and the cross.
- Chapters 5 and 6: immorality and lawsuits among believers.
- Chapter 7: marriage and singleness.
- Chapters 8 to 10: food offered to idols, and the limits of Christian freedom.
- Chapters 11 to 14: order in worship, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, and the way of love.
- Chapter 15: the resurrection of Christ and of believers.
- Chapter 16: the collection for Jerusalem, and greetings.
## What to look for

Each problem is answered by returning to the gospel. Chapter 13, the famous hymn to love, is placed in the middle of a discussion about gifts, to say that the gifts mean nothing without love. Chapter 15 is the earliest and fullest account of the resurrection, and it makes everything depend on it. The tone moves between sharp rebuke and warm affection.

The three letters of John are five chapters, one chapter and one chapter. They are among the simplest in vocabulary and among the deepest in thought. They are written in short sentences, with pairs of opposites: light and darkness, love and hate, truth and lies, life and death.

The letters do not name their author, but the early church was nearly unanimous in saying that they came from the apostle John, in his old age, probably in Ephesus around AD 85 to 95. They share a style and vocabulary with the Gospel of John. The first was written to a community shaken by a split, in which some who had left were denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh.
## How it is arranged
First John circles back to the same themes three times, rather than following a strict outline.

- 1:1 to 2:27: walking in the light, confessing sin, obeying the commandments, and warnings about antichrists.
- 2:28 to 4:6: children of God, who practice righteousness and love, and the test of spirits.
- 4:7 to 5:21: God is love, faith overcomes the world, and the assurance of eternal life.
- Second John: a short letter warning against hospitality to teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh.
- Third John: a note to Gaius, praising his hospitality to traveling missionaries and rebuking Diotrephes.
## What to look for

The author says why he writes: "so that you may know that you have eternal life." The tests of real faith are belief in Jesus as God's Son come in the flesh, obedience, and love for other believers. The letter gives two short definitions of God: "God is light" and "God is love." Love is shown most plainly in the sending of his Son.

First and Second Kings were also a single scroll, and they have forty-seven chapters between them. They carry the story of Israel from David's death to the fall of Jerusalem, about four centuries from about 970 BC to 586 BC. They pass judgment on each king by one measure: did he lead the people to worship the LORD alone?

The author is unnamed. Jewish tradition says Jeremiah, which is possible because his ministry overlaps the last events. The last event mentioned, the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon, took place about 561 BC (2 Kings 25:27-30), so the final form dates to the exile or soon after.
## How it is arranged

- 1 Kings 1 to 11: Solomon's reign, the building of the temple, and his decline.
- 1 Kings 12 to 2 Kings 17: the divided kingdom. The north falls to Assyria in 722 BC. The prophets Elijah and Elisha appear.
- 2 Kings 18 to 25: Judah alone. The reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, then the Babylonian invasion and the destruction of Jerusalem.
## What to look for

Kings explains why the exile happened, in the language of the covenant at Sinai and the warnings in Deuteronomy. It is not a neutral chronicle. It selects what matters for faith, which is why Omri, an important king politically, gets only a few verses. Yet the last scene is a flicker of hope. The line of David is not extinguished. A descendant is alive and honored in Babylon, which is the Bible's way of saying that God has not finished.

First Peter has five chapters and is a letter of encouragement to Christians who were suffering for their faith. It is addressed to believers scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor, whom Peter calls the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion. They did not belong anywhere, and the letter tells them who they really are.

The author is Peter the apostle, writing with the help of Silvanus, who is probably the same as Silas (5:12). He writes from "Babylon," which was a common code word for Rome, probably in the early 60s AD, as the persecution of Christians was beginning under Nero. The tone is hopeful, as of a man who has himself learned how to suffer.
## How it is arranged

- 1:1 to 2:10: the believers' new birth and living hope, and their identity as living stones, a holy priesthood and a chosen people.
- 2:11 to 3:12: living well among unbelievers, in society, at work and in the home, following the example of Christ in suffering.
- 3:13 to 5:14: how to face suffering, prepared to give a reason for hope, and humility and watchfulness for the elders and the young.
## What to look for

Peter's message is that suffering is not strange for those who follow Christ, and that it is not meaningless. The letter points again and again to the example of Jesus, and to the hope of an inheritance that cannot perish. A key verse is 3:15: "Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you." The instruction is to do it with gentleness and respect.

First and Second Samuel were originally a single scroll, divided in the Greek translation because of its length. Together they have fifty-five chapters. They are named for Samuel, the last judge and the prophet who anointed Israel's first two kings, though he dies in 1 Samuel 25 and is not the author of the later chapters.

The books do not say who wrote them. The writer used earlier records, and the work seems to have been put together some time after the kingdom split in 931 BC. The story covers about a century, from the birth of Samuel around 1100 BC to the end of David's reign around 970 BC.
## How it is arranged

- 1 Samuel 1 to 7: Samuel's birth and ministry, and the loss and return of the ark.
- 1 Samuel 8 to 15: Israel demands a king, and Saul is anointed, then rejected.
- 1 Samuel 16 to 31: David is anointed, kills Goliath, serves Saul, flees from him, and Saul dies.
- 2 Samuel 1 to 10: David becomes king, takes Jerusalem, and receives God's covenant promise.
- 2 Samuel 11 to 20: David's sin with Bathsheba and the family disasters that follow.
- 2 Samuel 21 to 24: appendices, including David's last songs and the census.
## What to look for

These books ask what a king should be. Saul looks the part but will not obey. David is flawed but repentant, and God makes the promise of an eternal throne to him in 2 Samuel 7, which is the hinge of the whole Old Testament. Watch how the LORD judges the heart and not the outward appearance. Hannah's song at the start and David's song near the end are meant to frame the books, and Mary's song in Luke 1 echoes the first.

First Thessalonians has five chapters and is probably the earliest of Paul's surviving letters, or very near it. It was written to a young church, which Paul had been forced to leave after only a few weeks, and it is filled with encouragement and affection. Reading it feels like a letter from a father to his children.

Paul, Silas and Timothy planted the church in Thessalonica, a major city in Macedonia, on the second journey (Acts 17), around AD 50. The new believers were harassed by their neighbors. Paul wrote from Corinth about AD 50 or 51 after Timothy returned with good news of their faith and love, together with some questions.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 3: thanksgiving for their faith, love and hope, a reminder of how Paul and his friends lived among them, and his joy at Timothy's report.
- Chapter 4: how to please God, with holiness and love, and teaching about those who have died.
- Chapter 5: the day of the Lord, and brief commands about community life.
## What to look for

The three words that begin the letter, faith, love and hope, are the framework. The most famous section is 4:13 to 18, where Paul comforts those who are grieving: Christ will return, the dead in Christ will rise first, and believers will be with the Lord forever. The letter says the church should live in watchfulness and joy, in the expectation of the coming of Jesus. It ends with the short commands "Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance."

First Timothy has six chapters and is the first of three letters, with Second Timothy and Titus, known as the Pastoral Letters, because they give guidance to leaders who care for churches. Timothy was Paul's young protégé, whom Paul calls his true child in the faith, and he had been left in Ephesus to deal with false teachers.

The traditional view is that Paul wrote after his release from the imprisonment described at the end of Acts, probably around AD 62 to 64. Some modern scholars think the Pastoral Letters were written in Paul's name by a follower after his death, citing their vocabulary and the church order they assume. Others reply that the letters are personal in a way a forger would hardly have achieved.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: false teaching and Paul's own testimony as a forgiven persecutor.
- Chapter 2: prayer for all, and order in worship.
- Chapter 3: qualifications for overseers and deacons, and the church as the household of God.
- Chapters 4 to 6: a warning about those who forbid marriage and certain foods, advice on caring for widows and elders, and warnings about the love of money.
## What to look for

Paul says that a leader should be above reproach in character, and the long lists in chapter 3 are mostly about behavior and not about gifts. The letter is concerned with sound teaching, and it repeatedly says that godliness is the point. The warning about money has become a classic: "the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil." The letter also holds a short early hymn about Christ in 3:16.

Second Corinthians has thirteen chapters and is Paul's most personal letter. He opens his heart about his sufferings, his weakness and his anxiety for a church that had turned against him. It shows what the apostle was like when he was not writing theology.

It was written from Macedonia, probably in AD 55 or 56, after a painful visit to Corinth and a severe letter that is now lost. Titus had brought good news of the church's repentance, and Paul writes with relief. Some scholars think that chapters 10 to 13, which change tone, were part of a different letter, but the manuscripts have always carried them together.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 7: Paul's ministry. God's comfort in affliction, the new covenant, treasure in clay jars, and the ministry of reconciliation.
- Chapters 8 and 9: the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and the principles of generous giving.
- Chapters 10 to 13: Paul defends his apostleship against rivals, whom he calls "super-apostles," and describes his "thorn in my flesh."
## What to look for

The theme is power in weakness. "We have this treasure in jars of clay," Paul says, "to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us." He is told in answer to prayer, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness." Chapter 5 explains the heart of the gospel: God reconciled the world to himself in Christ, and we are given the message of reconciliation.

Second Peter has three chapters and is a short farewell letter in which the apostle warns against false teachers and encourages growth in the faith. It speaks as the testament of a man who knows he will soon die, and it urges the readers to remember what they have been taught.

The letter names Simon Peter as the author and speaks of his coming death (1:14), which would place it in the mid-60s AD. It is the most disputed letter in the New Testament. It was accepted slowly by the early church, its style differs from 1 Peter, and many scholars think it was written later in Peter's name. Others defend Peter's authorship and the differences of style by the use of a different secretary.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: God's power has given everything for life and godliness, so add to faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, perseverance and love. Peter recalls the transfiguration and the reliability of prophecy.
- Chapter 2: false teachers who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, with examples of judgment from the Old Testament. This chapter is closely parallel to Jude.
- Chapter 3: scoffers who ask where the promised coming is, and the answer that the Lord is patient and the day will come.
## What to look for

The letter says Scripture did not come from human will, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. In chapter 3 Peter calls Paul's letters Scripture, which is an important early note. When people ask why Christ has not yet returned, the answer is that "with the Lord a day is like a thousand years," and that he does not delay but is patient, wanting everyone to come to repentance.

Second Thessalonians has three chapters and is a short follow-up to the first letter, written a few months later to the same church. Some of the believers had been unsettled by the claim that the day of the Lord had already come, and others had stopped working and were living off the generosity of others.

Paul, Silas and Timothy are named at the start, and the letter was probably written from Corinth in AD 51. A few scholars have questioned whether Paul wrote it, citing differences of tone from the first letter, but the traditional view remains the majority one.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: thanks for their steadfast faith under persecution, and the promise that Christ will bring justice at his return.
- Chapter 2: the day of the Lord has not yet come. First, the rebellion and the revealing of "the man of lawlessness" must happen.
- Chapter 3: a request for prayer, and a strong word to those who live in idleness.
## What to look for

Chapter 2 is among the most difficult passages in Paul, and Christians have disagreed for centuries about who or what the man of lawlessness and the restrainer are. The main point is clear and practical. Believers should not be shaken by claims that the end has come, and they should keep working. Paul says, "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat," and he tells them to hold to the teachings they were given.

Second Timothy has four chapters and is the last letter Paul wrote. It was composed from a Roman prison, where, unlike in his earlier imprisonments, he expected to die. It is a farewell to the younger man whom he loved, and it is among the most moving writings in the New Testament.

Paul was probably executed under the emperor Nero, around AD 64 to 67, according to early church tradition. The letter says that most of his friends in Asia had deserted him, that only Luke was with him, and that he wanted Timothy to come quickly, and to bring his cloak and his books.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: a charge to fan into flame the gift of God, and not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul in chains.
- Chapter 2: images of a soldier, an athlete and a farmer, and a call to be faithful with what has been entrusted.
- Chapter 3: difficult times ahead, and a reminder that Scripture is God-breathed and equips for every good work.
- Chapter 4: a solemn charge to preach the word, Paul's own final summary, and personal greetings.
## What to look for

Paul writes as one who is passing the baton: "Guard the treasure entrusted to you." His summary of his life is one of the great sentences of the Bible: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." He is not afraid. The letter says that the word of God is not chained, and that the Lord stood by him and gave him strength.

Acts has twenty-eight chapters and is the second volume of Luke's work, the only narrative book in the New Testament after the Gospels. Its full title, Acts of the Apostles, is a little misleading, since it focuses on Peter in the first half and Paul in the second. Many have said that it is better named the acts of the Holy Spirit through the apostles.

Luke wrote it, and in some stretches he uses "we," showing that he was present as a companion of Paul. The book ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, probably around AD 60 to 62, which suggests it was finished about then, though some date it later. It covers about thirty years, from the ascension of Jesus about AD 30 to Paul's two years in Rome.
## How it is arranged
Acts 1:8 gives the outline: witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

- Chapters 1 to 7: Jerusalem. The ascension, Pentecost, the early church, persecution, and the death of Stephen.
- Chapters 8 to 12: Judea and Samaria and beyond. Philip, Saul's conversion, Peter and Cornelius, and the church at Antioch.
- Chapters 13 to 20: Paul's three missionary journeys, and the council at Jerusalem in chapter 15.
- Chapters 21 to 28: Paul arrested in Jerusalem, tried before governors and a king, shipwrecked, and brought to Rome.
## What to look for

Watch the Spirit: he comes at Pentecost, falls on Samaritans and Gentiles, and sends out missionaries. Watch how the gospel crosses boundaries of culture and language. The ending is deliberate. Paul is in chains, and yet "boldly and freely he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ." The word of God is not bound, and the story goes on.

Amos has nine chapters and is the book of a farmer who became a prophet. Amos was a shepherd and a grower of sycamore figs from Tekoa, in Judah, who was sent north to Israel, where he spoke in the days of Jeroboam II and Uzziah, around 760 BC. It was a boom time, with prosperity for the wealthy and misery for the poor.

His book is among the earliest prophetic writings. It begins with a sharp rhetorical trap: he announces judgment on Israel's neighbors, so that his listeners will nod along, and then he turns to Israel itself.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 and 2: judgment on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, and finally Israel.
- Chapters 3 to 6: three sermons that begin with "Hear this word," on injustice, empty worship and false security.
- Chapters 7 to 9: five visions, including a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit, with the clash between Amos and the priest Amaziah, and a closing promise of restoration.
## What to look for

Amos is the prophet of justice. He denounces those who sell the needy for a pair of sandals and trample the poor, and he says God despises religious festivals that are not matched by right living. His most quoted line is the call to let justice roll down like waters. Yet the book ends with hope: God will rebuild David's fallen shelter, and James quotes the passage at the council in Jerusalem to show that the Gentiles are to be included (Acts 15:16-17).

Colossians has four chapters and is a short letter that sets out the supremacy of Christ over everything. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus Valley, in what is now Turkey, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never been there. The church was started by his associate Epaphras, who came to him in prison with a worrying report.

It was written from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60 to 62, and it was carried by Tychicus along with the letters to Philemon and to the Ephesians, which share much of its wording. The false teaching at Colossae is not fully described, but it seems to have mixed Jewish rules about food and festivals with a mystical philosophy, the worship of angels and a belief that Christ was not enough. A few scholars doubt Paul's authorship, though many accept it.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: thanks and prayer, then a great hymn to Christ as the image of the invisible God, the creator and reconciler of all things.
- Chapter 2: warnings against empty philosophy and human rules. In Christ all the fullness of deity lives in bodily form.
- Chapters 3 and 4: new life with Christ. Set your minds on things above, put off the old self, put on love, and live out the new life in households, and in prayer and speech.
## What to look for

The answer to every false teaching is Christ. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. The believer is not looking for anything more, because "you have been made complete in Christ." The consequence is a new way of life, in which the old habits are stripped off like dirty clothes and a new character put on.

Daniel has twelve chapters and is a book of two halves. The first six tell stories of Daniel and his friends, who stay faithful in the court of a foreign empire. The last six record visions that Daniel received about the future of the world's kingdoms. It is the model for the later Jewish and Christian writings that scholars call apocalyptic.

The book places Daniel in Babylon from 605 BC, and it ends in the reign of Cyrus. Tradition has held that Daniel wrote it in the sixth century BC. Many critical scholars date it to about 165 BC, during the persecution by Antiochus Epiphanes, because of its detailed accounts of the Seleucid kings and because of certain words in the text. Conservative scholars reply that the language and setting fit the sixth century and that God can reveal the future. This is among the most contested questions in Old Testament studies.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: Daniel and three friends are trained in Nebuchadnezzar's court.
- Chapters 2 to 6: the statue dream, the fiery furnace, the king's madness, the writing on the wall and the lions' den. The text from 2:4 to 7:28 is in Aramaic, not Hebrew.
- Chapters 7 to 12: visions of four beasts and the Son of Man, a ram and a goat, the seventy weeks, and the final conflict and resurrection.
## What to look for

The theme is that God rules the kingdoms of the earth. Empires rise and fall, but "His dominion is an everlasting dominion." Notice how the heroes handle pressure with courage and with respect. In chapter 7 One "like the Son of Man" comes before God and receives an everlasting kingdom, a title Jesus uses for himself more than any other. Chapter 12 holds one of the clearest Old Testament promises of resurrection.

Deuteronomy has thirty-four chapters. Its name means "second law" in Greek, a mistranslation of a phrase meaning a copy of this instruction, but the title fits, since Moses restates the law to a new generation on the plains of Moab. The Hebrew title, Devarim, simply means "Words."

Tradition holds that Moses spoke and wrote it just before his death, with a later hand adding the account of his burial in chapter 34. Many scholars connect the book with the reforms of King Josiah in the seventh century BC, in which "the Book of the Law" was found in the temple. Its form closely follows that of ancient treaties between kings and their subjects, which suggests that it is deliberately a covenant document.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 4: Moses looks back on the journey from Sinai and urges obedience.
- Chapters 5 to 11: the Ten Commandments repeated, the Shema, and the call to love God wholeheartedly.
- Chapters 12 to 26: detailed laws about worship, justice, family, and care for the poor.
- Chapters 27 to 30: blessings and curses, and the covenant renewal.
- Chapters 31 to 34: Joshua commissioned, Moses' song and blessing, and his death on Mount Nebo.
## What to look for

Deuteronomy asks for love, not just rule keeping: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart." It stresses remembering, teaching children and choosing life. It also predicts that Israel will fail and be scattered, and then be brought back, which is why later prophets keep quoting it. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy three times to answer the devil in the wilderness (Matthew 4), and he calls the Shema's command the greatest of all.

Ecclesiastes has twelve chapters and is the most puzzling of the wisdom books. The title is the Greek form of the Hebrew Qoheleth, usually translated "the Preacher" or "the Teacher," a word that comes from a root meaning to gather an assembly. The book is his sustained meditation on life "under the sun."

The writer calls himself "son of David, king in Jerusalem," which is traditionally taken as Solomon. Many modern scholars, noting the style of the Hebrew, place the final form later, in the Persian period. Those who accept Solomon point to his wealth and wisdom, which the book claims. Either way, the book is presented as the Teacher's hard-won conclusions.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 and 2: the search for meaning in wisdom, pleasure and achievement, all of which prove to be vapor.
- Chapters 3 to 6: time and eternity, injustice, work, wealth and the limits of what people can know.
- Chapters 7 to 10: practical wisdom, with proverbs about folly and advice for a confusing world.
- Chapters 11 and 12: live boldly and joyfully, remember your Creator while you are young, and fear God.
## What to look for

The famous word is hevel, "vapor," "breath," or "meaningless," which appears nearly forty times. It does not mean nothing matters. It means that life is fleeting and cannot be grasped or controlled. The Teacher says that the answer is not to give up but to receive each day's food, work and love as a gift from God. The book ends with the conclusion that to fear God and keep his commandments is the whole duty of man, and Paul's remark that creation was subjected to futility (Romans 8:20) echoes this book.

Ephesians has six chapters and is a letter about the grandeur of the church and the riches of life in Christ. It reads more like a sermon or a meditation than a reply to a problem, and it is often called the crown of Paul's letters. It falls neatly in two: three chapters about what God has done, and three about how to live in light of it.

Paul wrote it from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60 to 62. Some of the oldest manuscripts leave out the words "in Ephesus" in the first verse, which has led many to think it was a circular letter meant for a group of churches in Asia Minor, with Ephesus as one stop. A number of scholars doubt that Paul wrote it, citing its long sentences and vocabulary, but most Christians through history have accepted it as his.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 3: praise for every spiritual blessing in Christ, salvation by grace through faith, the joining of Jews and Gentiles into one body, and a prayer that believers may know the love of Christ.
- Chapters 4 to 6: unity and maturity in the church, putting off the old self, walking in love and light, the marriage and household codes, and the armor of God.
## What to look for

Count how often the letter says "in Christ" or "in him." Chapter 2 gives the best-known summary: "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God." The theme that holds it together is the mystery now revealed, that Gentiles are fellow heirs with Jews. The church is a body, a building, and a bride, and its life together is meant to show God's wisdom to the world.

Esther has ten chapters and is the story of a Jewish orphan who becomes queen of Persia and saves her people. It is set in the capital at Susa during the reign of Ahasuerus, who is identified with Xerxes I, around 483 to 473 BC. It is the book of the Bible in which God is never named, and that is deliberate.

The author is unknown. Jewish tradition has suggested Mordecai or Ezra. The details of Persian court life are accurate and the writer was clearly familiar with the empire, so the book was probably written not long after the events. The Jews still read it aloud each year at the feast of Purim.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 and 2: the queen Vashti is dismissed, and Esther is chosen as queen.
- Chapters 3 to 5: Haman, the king's chief minister, plots to destroy all the Jews. Esther decides to approach the king uninvited.
- Chapters 6 to 8: the tables turn. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, and the Jews are allowed to defend themselves.
- Chapters 9 and 10: the Jews are saved, and Purim is established.
## What to look for

The hidden hand of God is the point. Coincidences stack up, from the queen's selection to the king's sleepless night, and Mordecai's challenge gives the book its center: "who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Esther is a reminder that even when God seems absent, he is at work, and that faith sometimes means taking a risk.

Exodus, the second book, has forty chapters. The English title is the Greek word for "departure," and it names the event at the center of the Old Testament, the rescue of Israel from slavery in Egypt. The Hebrew title, Shemot, means "Names," from its opening words listing the sons of Jacob who came down to Egypt.

By tradition Moses is the author, and the book itself says he wrote down some of what happened (Exodus 24:4). The date of the exodus is debated. The early view puts it about 1446 BC, based on 1 Kings 6:1, and the later one about 1260 BC, based on the Egyptian city Rameses mentioned in Exodus 1:11.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 15: slavery, the call of Moses at the burning bush, the ten plagues, the first Passover and the crossing of the sea.
- Chapters 15 to 18: the first weeks in the wilderness, with bitter water, manna and quail, and water from the rock.
- Chapters 19 to 24: the covenant at Sinai, with the Ten Commandments and the laws that follow.
- Chapters 25 to 40: the tabernacle, the golden calf and its aftermath, and the glory of the LORD filling the tent.
## What to look for

The book is about redemption and presence. God saves first and then gives the law, and he saves in order to live among his people. The name he reveals at the bush, "I AM WHO I AM," is the name the rest of the Bible keeps returning to. Look for the Passover lamb, the mediator who goes up the mountain, the bread from heaven and the tent of meeting. The New Testament reads every one of them as pointing to Jesus.

Ezekiel has forty-eight chapters and is the strangest of the major prophets, full of visions, symbolic acts and detailed plans. Its name means "God strengthens." The book is dated with unusual care, by the year of King Jehoiachin's exile, which makes it the easiest of the prophets to place on a timeline.

Ezekiel was a priest who was carried off to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and he began to prophesy in 593 BC at about the age of thirty, by the Kebar canal. The latest dated passage is from 571 BC. He lived among the exiles, while Jeremiah was warning those who stayed in Jerusalem, and the two messages match.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 3: the vision of the glory of the LORD on a moving throne and Ezekiel's call as a watchman.
- Chapters 4 to 24: judgment on Jerusalem, with symbolic acts and the departure of the glory from the temple.
- Chapters 25 to 32: oracles against the surrounding nations.
- Chapters 33 to 39: news of the fall, then promises of a new shepherd, a new heart, the dry bones and the defeat of Gog.
- Chapters 40 to 48: a vision of a new temple and a river of life, ending with the name of the city: "The LORD is there."
## What to look for

Ezekiel says again and again, "Then they will know that I am the LORD." Judgment and restoration both serve that end. The great promise in chapter 36 is a new heart and God's Spirit within his people, which many readers hear behind Jesus' words to Nicodemus about being born of water and the Spirit. The last chapters, with a river flowing from the temple, feed into the picture of the river of life in Revelation 22.

Ezra and Nehemiah are two books, with ten and thirteen chapters, that in the Hebrew Bible form one scroll. They tell what happened when the Jews came home from Babylon, and they are the last historical books of the Old Testament in time.

Tradition credits Ezra with writing the book that bears his name, and Nehemiah's own memoirs are quoted in the second book, in the first person. Together they cover roughly a century, from the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC to Nehemiah's second term as governor after 433 BC.
## How it is arranged

- Ezra 1 to 6: the return under Zerubbabel and the rebuilding of the temple, completed in 516 BC.
- Ezra 7 to 10: Ezra arrives in 458 BC and addresses marriages with foreign women.
- Nehemiah 1 to 7: Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, rebuilds the wall of Jerusalem in fifty-two days, despite opposition.
- Nehemiah 8 to 10: Ezra reads the Law to the people, and they renew the covenant.
- Nehemiah 11 to 13: the city is repopulated and the wall dedicated, followed by Nehemiah's reforms.
## What to look for

The books show how to rebuild when everything has been lost. They are full of prayer. Nehemiah prays before speaking to the king and again under attack, and Ezra prays over the people's sin. They also stress the Word of God: when the law is read, the people weep, and then Nehemiah tells them that the joy of the LORD is their strength. The final lesson is that reform is never finished, which is why Nehemiah ends with a prayer.

Galatians has six chapters and is a short and passionate letter, written in anger. Paul has heard that some teachers are telling his Gentile converts that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved, and he writes at once. It is the charter of Christian freedom, and the clearest statement in the New Testament that people are put right with God by faith and not by works of the law.

The date is debated. If "Galatia" means the southern region where Paul planted churches on his first journey (Acts 13 and 14), the letter could be as early as AD 48, before the council at Jerusalem. If it means the northern region, it would be about AD 53 to 55. Either way it is among the earliest of Paul's letters.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 and 2: Paul defends his gospel and his apostleship, including how he confronted Peter at Antioch.
- Chapters 3 and 4: the argument from Abraham, who was counted righteous by faith, and from the purpose of the law, which was a guardian until Christ came.
- Chapters 5 and 6: freedom in Christ, life by the Spirit, the fruit of the Spirit, and bearing one another's burdens.
## What to look for

Paul is blunt: anyone who preaches another gospel should be cursed. The center is 2:20, "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me." The letter says that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, and it ends with the fruit of the Spirit, which is the life of freedom.

Genesis, the first book of the Bible, has fifty chapters. The English name comes from the Greek word for "origin," while Jews call it Bereshit, "In the beginning," after its first word. It is a book of beginnings: of the world, of marriage, of sin and death, of nations and languages, and of the family through which God chose to bless them.

Jewish and Christian tradition has held that Moses wrote Genesis along with the next four books, probably during the wilderness years, which would place it in the fifteenth or thirteenth century BC depending on the date of the exodus. Many modern scholars think the Pentateuch grew over centuries from older sources and was given its final shape around or after the exile. Whichever view you take, the book presents itself as a single story, and the church has read it that way.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 11: the beginnings of the whole human family. Creation, the fall, Cain and Abel, the flood, and Babel.
- Chapters 12 to 25: Abraham, called to leave his home and trust God's promise of a land, a nation and a blessing.
- Chapters 25 to 36: Isaac and Jacob, whose family gives the nation its name, Israel.
- Chapters 37 to 50: Joseph, sold into Egypt, who rises to save the family from famine.
## What to look for

Watch the promise. God speaks it to Abraham in chapter 12, repeats it to Isaac and Jacob, and keeps it alive through barren wives, family feuds and famine. The book is honest about its heroes, and the credit goes to God. It also plants seeds that the rest of Scripture harvests: the promise of a seed who will crush the serpent, the blessing to all nations, and a ruler from Judah. Genesis ends with Joseph's coffin in Egypt and a hope of going home.

Habakkuk has three chapters and is the book of a prophet who argues with God. Unlike most prophets, he is not speaking to the people for God, but to God for the people. The name may come from a word meaning "embrace" or "wrestle," which suits him.

He wrote when Babylon was rising to power, probably about 605 BC, a time when Judah was full of violence and injustice. Habakkuk asks how long God will tolerate it, and God says he is raising up the Babylonians. That answer is worse than the problem, and Habakkuk objects again.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: the first complaint, God's answer that Babylon is coming, and the second complaint.
- Chapters 2:1 to 20: Habakkuk waits at his post, and God answers with a vision and five woes against the proud.
- Chapter 3: a prayer in the form of a psalm, recalling God's past rescues, and ending in a song of trust.
## What to look for

The center is a single sentence, "the righteous will live by faith" (2:4). It means that those who are right with God keep living by faithfulness, trusting him even when things seem to go wrong. Paul quotes it in Romans and Galatians, and Hebrews quotes it too, to mean that justification is by faith. The book ends with Habakkuk saying that even if everything fails, he will rejoice in the LORD, who is the God of his salvation.

Haggai has two chapters and is the second shortest book in the Old Testament after Obadiah, though it is one of the best dated. Its four messages are each dated to the day, between August and December of 520 BC, in the second year of the Persian king Darius.

The returned exiles had begun to rebuild the temple in 536 BC, then stopped, discouraged by opposition and by their own concerns. Sixteen years later they were living in comfortable houses while the house of God lay in ruins. Haggai and his younger contemporary Zechariah told them to start again. The people obeyed, and the work was completed in 516 BC.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: "Consider your ways." The people are told to rebuild, and they respond within weeks.
- Chapter 2:1 to 9: the new temple seems small, but God promises that its glory will be greater.
- Chapter 2:10 to 19: a question about holiness and defilement, and a promise of blessing from that day.
- Chapter 2:20 to 23: a message to Zerubbabel, the descendant of David, as God's chosen servant.
## What to look for

Haggai is about priorities. People who put their own comfort ahead of God's work find that they are never satisfied, and when they start working, God says, "I am with you." The book also looks forward. God promises to shake the heavens and the earth, and Hebrews 12:26-28 uses that promise to speak of a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

Hebrews has thirteen chapters and is a carefully written sermon about the superiority of Jesus Christ to everything that came before. It is the most polished Greek in the New Testament and one of the most theologically rich books, and it explains the Old Testament sacrifices and priesthood by showing how Christ fulfills them.

The author is unknown. The letter does not name him. Origen, a third-century scholar, said that only God knows who wrote it. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, Priscilla and Luke have all been suggested. It was written to Jewish Christians who were under pressure and tempted to turn back, probably before AD 70, because it speaks as if the temple services were still going on.
## How it is arranged

- 1:1 to 4:13: Christ is greater than the prophets, angels and Moses, and a warning against unbelief.
- 4:14 to 10:18: Christ is the great high priest, in the order of Melchizedek, with a better covenant and a better sacrifice, offered once for all.
- 10:19 to 12:29: draw near with confidence, hold on, and run with endurance, with the great roll of those who lived by faith in chapter 11.
- Chapter 13: practical exhortations and a blessing.
## What to look for

The word "better" runs through it: a better hope, a better covenant, better promises. The letter contains five stern warnings against drifting away, and Christians have debated how to read them. It also gives the best-known definition of faith in the Bible, in chapter 11. And it offers the picture of Jesus as the one who understands our weakness, so that we may "approach the throne of grace with confidence."

Hosea has fourteen chapters and is the first of the twelve Minor Prophets. His name means "salvation," and it is the same name as Joshua. Hosea is the story of a prophet whose own broken marriage becomes a picture of God's relationship to Israel.

He prophesied in the northern kingdom from about 755 BC until shortly before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, a time of political chaos in which several kings were assassinated. He was a contemporary of Amos in the north and of Isaiah and Micah in the south. The book is personal and emotional, and the prophet's voice breaks off, turns, and returns.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 3: Hosea marries Gomer, who proves unfaithful. He buys her back. Their children are given names that carry a message.
- Chapters 4 to 14: oracles against Israel's idolatry and injustice, alternating between charge, judgment and tender appeals, and closing with a call to return.
## What to look for

The key Hebrew word is chesed, loyal love, the covenant love of God that does not let go. God compares himself to a husband whose wife has gone, and to a father teaching a child to walk (11:3). Judgment is real, but it is never the last word: "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" (11:8). Matthew applies Hosea 11:1 to Jesus coming out of Egypt, and Paul quotes the book to show how God calls those who were not his people.

Isaiah has sixty-six chapters and is the longest of the prophetic books, sometimes called the fifth gospel because of how often the New Testament quotes it. Isaiah's name means "the LORD saves," and the book is about salvation in a world of judgment.

Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 BC, in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Many scholars think chapters 40 to 66 come from the time of the exile and after, and refer to a later prophet or school. Others hold that one prophet wrote the whole book and foresaw the exile and Cyrus. The great Isaiah scroll found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, about a thousand years older than any other complete copy, shows the book already in its full form by about 125 BC.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 12: the call of Isaiah, warnings to Judah, and promises of a future king, the child Immanuel.
- Chapters 13 to 35: oracles to the nations and woes against faithless leaders, with visions of the future kingdom.
- Chapters 36 to 39: a historical bridge, in which Hezekiah faces the Assyrians and then Babylon.
- Chapters 40 to 55: comfort for the exiles and the Servant of the LORD, culminating in chapters 52 and 53.
- Chapters 56 to 66: the future of God's people, ending with a new heavens and a new earth.
## What to look for

Isaiah's favorite name for God is "the Holy One of Israel." The book holds judgment and hope together, and it keeps pointing to a coming king and a suffering servant. Look at how chapters 7, 9 and 11 speak of the king and chapter 53 of the servant who bears sin. Jesus read from Isaiah 61 at Nazareth. The ending, with the new creation in chapters 65 and 66, is picked up in Revelation.

James has five chapters and reads like the wisdom literature of the Old Testament in a Christian voice. It is a practical letter, more like Proverbs than Romans, with short, direct commands about speech, money, patience and prayer. Martin Luther disliked it at first, because it seemed to him to contradict Paul, but later readers have seen that the two are addressing different problems.

The author calls himself "a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ," and the tradition identifies him as James, the brother of Jesus, who became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15) and was martyred about AD 62. Some think it was written as early as the mid-40s AD, which would make it among the earliest books in the New Testament. It is addressed to Jewish Christians scattered abroad.
## How it is arranged
James moves quickly from topic to topic, but the main themes are these.

- Chapter 1: trials as a means of maturity, asking God for wisdom, and being doers of the word.
- Chapter 2: against showing favoritism to the rich, and the relationship between faith and works.
- Chapter 3: the power of the tongue, and the wisdom that comes from above.
- Chapters 4 and 5: warnings against pride and worldliness, a rebuke to the rich who oppress workers, patience, and prayer for the sick.
## What to look for

The famous passage is 2:14 to 26: "faith without deeds is dead." James is not arguing against justification by faith. He is saying that real faith produces real obedience. The tests he gives are concrete: how you speak, how you treat the poor, whether you control your anger, whether you hear and do.

Judges has twenty-one chapters and tells of Israel's life between the death of Joshua and the rise of the monarchy. A judge in this book is less a courtroom official than a military and moral leader raised up by God for a time of crisis. The book is the darkest in the Former Prophets, and it ends on a note of ruin.

Its author is unknown. Jewish tradition suggests Samuel. The repeated line that "in those days there was no king in Israel" suggests it was written once the monarchy had begun, perhaps in the time of David or later. The events fill the years between the entry into Canaan and about 1050 BC, when Saul became king.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 2: the incomplete conquest and an explanation of why the people fell into trouble.
- Chapters 3 to 16: the stories of the judges. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Abimelech, Jephthah and Samson.
- Chapters 17 to 21: two appalling stories of idolatry and violence, which show how far Israel has sunk.
## What to look for

The pattern repeats in cycles of sin, oppression, a cry for help, rescue and rest, and each loop sinks lower. The leaders also decline, from faithful Othniel to flawed Gideon and then to Samson, who lives for himself. The book is meant to make the reader hungry for something better. By the end you are asking for a king who will do right, and then, as the Bible goes on, for a king who will do more than any human king could.

Jeremiah has fifty-two chapters and is one of the longest books in the Bible. It is the record of a prophet who lived through the end of Judah and who suffered for telling people the truth about it. It is deeply personal. Jeremiah's own prayers and complaints are woven in as in no other prophet.

Jeremiah was a priest from Anathoth, called about 627 BC under King Josiah, and he prophesied until after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. His scribe Baruch wrote down his words (chapter 36). The material is not in order of date, since it was arranged by theme and by the way the book was edited, which can confuse a new reader.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: Jeremiah's call.
- Chapters 2 to 25: warnings and calls to repent, with images of the potter, the broken jar and the linen belt, and the "temple sermon."
- Chapters 26 to 29: conflict with false prophets, and the letter to the exiles.
- Chapters 30 to 33: the Book of Consolation, with the promise of the new covenant.
- Chapters 34 to 45: stories of the siege, the fall and the aftermath.
- Chapters 46 to 52: oracles against the nations, and an appendix about the fall.
## What to look for

Jeremiah's message is that outward religion without a changed heart cannot save. His own life is the sermon: he is not allowed to marry, he is thrown into a cistern, and he weeps over those he warns. The center of hope is the new covenant, in which God writes his law on hearts and forgives sins. Jesus calls the cup at the Last Supper the new covenant, and Hebrews 8 quotes the whole passage.

John has twenty-one chapters and stands apart from Matthew, Mark and Luke. It has almost no parables, but long conversations, such as those with Nicodemus and the woman at the well, and seven "signs," or miracles. Seven times Jesus makes an "I am" statement, such as "I am the bread of life" and "I am the good shepherd." Its first sentence goes back before creation, to the Word who was with God and was God.

Tradition names the apostle John son of Zebedee, "the disciple whom Jesus loved," as the author, writing late in life from Ephesus, perhaps in the 80s or 90s AD. The Gospel does not name him, and some scholars suggest it came from a circle around him or from another John, but the church has always valued its eyewitness character. Its purpose is stated near the end.
## How it is arranged

- 1:1 to 18: the prologue, about the Word who became flesh.
- 1:19 to 12:50: the Book of Signs. Seven miracles, from water into wine to the raising of Lazarus, with the teaching that goes with each.
- Chapters 13 to 17: the upper room, where Jesus washes the disciples' feet, gives his farewell teaching and prays.
- Chapters 18 to 21: the arrest, crucifixion, resurrection and an appearance by the lake.
## What to look for

John says why he wrote: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name." Watch for the great contrasts of light and darkness, life and death, belief and unbelief. The Gospel says very plainly that Jesus is God, from the opening verse to Thomas's cry, "My Lord and my God!"

Job has forty-two chapters and is one of the great books on suffering. It begins and ends in prose, and in between it is a long poem, a series of speeches. It belongs to the wisdom books, with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, and it takes on the hardest question those books raise: why do the innocent suffer?

The book does not say who wrote it or when. Job himself lives in the land of Uz, and the details of his life, such as his wealth counted in animals and his role as the family priest, resemble the patriarchal world of Genesis. The language of the poetry is rich and difficult. The date of writing is debated, and the book has no connection with the history of Israel as such.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 and 2: a righteous man loses his children, wealth and health, after a challenge from Satan in the court of heaven.
- Chapters 3 to 31: Job laments and argues with three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, who insist that he must have sinned.
- Chapters 32 to 37: a young man named Elihu offers a fourth view.
- Chapters 38 to 42: the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, and Job responds. He is restored.
## What to look for

Watch what the friends get wrong. They are certain that suffering always follows sin, and at the end God says they have not spoken rightly of him, while Job has (42:7). God's answer does not explain the reason for Job's pain. It shows him the scale of creation and asks whether Job understands how the world is run. The answer is a presence, not an argument. Job also glimpses a living Redeemer who will stand on the earth in the end (19:25), a hope Christians read in light of Christ.

Joel has three chapters in English Bibles, and it is a short prophecy about a plague of locusts and the day of the LORD. Its name means "the LORD is God." It is memorable for its images of an invading swarm and for a promise that Peter picked up on the day of Pentecost.

Nothing in the book gives a date. Joel mentions no kings, and scholars have suggested dates ranging from the ninth century BC to the fourth. The book was shaped around a real disaster, a locust plague, and it takes that disaster as a warning of a greater day that is coming.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: the locusts devastate the land, and the people are told to mourn.
- Chapter 2:1 to 17: the locusts are a picture of an army, and the prophet calls for a solemn assembly and repentance.
- Chapter 2:18 to 32: God answers with mercy, restores the harvest and promises to pour out his Spirit.
- Chapter 3: judgment on the nations and a vision of Judah's blessing.
## What to look for

Joel announces a God who is "gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion." The call is to tear hearts and not just clothes. The great promise in 2:28 is that God will pour out his Spirit on all people, so that sons and daughters, old and young, will prophesy. Peter says that this is what was happening on the day of Pentecost, and the book closes with the promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.

Jonah has four chapters and is the story of the reluctant prophet who ran from God's command and then resented God's mercy. It is the only prophetic book that is mostly narrative. Jonah son of Amittai is named in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet under Jeroboam II, in the eighth century BC.

Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, was the most feared city of the age. Jonah is told to go there and call it to repentance, and he gets on a ship for Tarshish, in the opposite direction. Christians have read the book in different ways. Most have taken it as a historical account, as Jesus seems to do when he speaks of "the sign of Jonah." Others see it as a parable or a satire, a story that makes a theological point. The book is meant to challenge its readers, whatever its form.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: Jonah flees, a storm strikes, and sailors throw him overboard. A great fish swallows him.
- Chapter 2: Jonah's prayer from inside the fish.
- Chapter 3: Jonah finally goes to Nineveh, and the city repents.
- Chapter 4: Jonah is angry at God's compassion, and God ends the book with a question.
## What to look for

The book is a mirror. The pagan sailors and the people of Nineveh respond quickly, and the prophet, the one who should know better, is the stubborn one. Jonah says why he ran: "I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion." He wanted the enemy judged and not forgiven. Jesus uses the three days in the fish as a sign of his resurrection, and says that the men of Nineveh will stand in judgment, because they repented at Jonah's preaching, and "One greater than Jonah is here."

Joshua has twenty-four chapters. It is named for the man who succeeded Moses and led Israel into Canaan. His name in Hebrew, Yehoshua, means "the LORD saves," and the Greek form of it is Jesus. The book picks up exactly where Deuteronomy leaves off, and together with Judges, Samuel and Kings it forms what Jewish tradition calls the Former Prophets.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition says Joshua wrote most of it, and the text itself says he wrote down the covenant renewal at Shechem (Joshua 24:26). The events would date to about 1400 BC on the early chronology or about 1250 to 1200 BC on the later one. The book was probably put into its present form somewhat later.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 5: preparations. Crossing the Jordan, circumcision of the new generation, and the Passover at Gilgal.
- Chapters 6 to 12: the conquest. Jericho, Ai, the Gibeonite treaty, and campaigns in the south and the north.
- Chapters 13 to 21: the land divided among the tribes, with cities of refuge and towns for the Levites.
- Chapters 22 to 24: the eastern tribes go home, and Joshua's farewell speeches and the covenant at Shechem.
## What to look for

The theme is that God keeps his word: "Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled" (Joshua 21:45). The book is also demanding. It requires faith in battle and loyalty in daily life, and the conquest accounts raise hard moral questions that Christians read carefully. Notice Rahab, a Canaanite who is saved by faith, and the "Commander of the LORD’s army" whom Joshua meets before Jericho.

Jude is one chapter of twenty-five verses and is a short, fierce letter about defending the faith. The writer had meant to write about salvation, but felt that he had to urge the readers instead "to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints."

The author calls himself "a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James," and the usual view is that he was the brother of Jesus, who like James had once doubted but later believed. The date is uncertain, from the 60s to the 80s AD. A large part of it closely resembles 2 Peter 2, and it is not clear which came first.
## How it is arranged

- Verses 1 to 4: greeting, and the reason for writing, which is that certain people have slipped into the church and are perverting grace.
- Verses 5 to 16: examples of judgment, from the exodus generation, the angels who left their post, and Sodom and Gomorrah, and a portrait of the false teachers.
- Verses 17 to 23: remember what the apostles said, build yourselves up, and show mercy to those who doubt.
- Verses 24 and 25: one of the finest doxologies in the Bible.
## What to look for

Jude draws on a Jewish book called 1 Enoch (verses 14 and 15) and on other Jewish traditions, which shows that a New Testament writer could quote a source without making all of it Scripture. The tone is urgent, but the end is joy. The closing blessing says that God "is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy."

Lamentations has five chapters, and it is a book of five poems of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem. The Hebrew title, Eikhah, "How," is the first word of the book, the cry of someone staring at a ruin: how the city sits alone. It is the Bible's funeral song for a city.

The book is anonymous. Greek and Latin tradition connect it to Jeremiah, who did write laments for Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:25), though nothing in the book says so. It was written after the fall of the city in 586 BC and probably within a generation, by someone who had seen it.
## How it is arranged
The first four poems are acrostics, in which each verse or group of verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, as if to say that all grief from A to Z is being put into words.

- Chapter 1: the city sits desolate, and no one comforts her.
- Chapter 2: God's anger against Zion, and the suffering of children.
- Chapter 3: the poet's personal pain, and a turn to hope at the center. This chapter has three verses for each letter.
- Chapter 4: the siege and its horrors, remembered.
- Chapter 5: a final prayer for restoration, not an acrostic but with twenty-two verses.
## What to look for

Lamentations gives permission to grieve. It does not rush to explain, and yet at the center it makes one of the great statements of faith: "Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail." The final lines ask God to restore his people, and they end with a question that is left open. The book teaches that faith can sit in the ashes, and still call God faithful.

Leviticus has twenty-seven chapters, and it is the instruction manual for life with God in the middle of the camp. Its English name comes from the Greek and Latin titles, which refer to the tribe of Levi, whose men served as priests and helpers in the sanctuary. Jews call it Vayikra, "And he called," from the first words.

The book is set at Sinai, at the foot of the mountain, between the building of the tabernacle at the end of Exodus and the departure at the beginning of Numbers. Tradition assigns it to Moses. Most of it is spoken by God directly, and the phrase "the LORD spoke to Moses" comes up over and over.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 7: the five main offerings (the burnt offering, grain offering, peace offering, sin offering and guilt offering) and how priests handle them.
- Chapters 8 to 10: the ordination of Aaron and his sons, and the death of two priests who offered unauthorized fire.
- Chapters 11 to 15: what is clean and unclean, including food, childbirth, skin disease and bodily discharges.
- Chapter 16: the Day of Atonement.
- Chapters 17 to 27: the call to holiness in daily life, including love for neighbor, festivals, the Sabbath year and the year of Jubilee.
## What to look for

Two ideas hold the book together: God is holy, and sin is costly. Sacrifices let a sinner come near without being consumed, and they teach that forgiveness takes a life. Hebrews explains that these were shadows, and that Christ is the final sacrifice and the true high priest. Notice also how much of the book is about ordinary things such as honest scales and care for foreigners. Holiness is not only for priests.

Luke has twenty-four chapters and is the longest Gospel by word count, and it is the first volume of a two-part work, with Acts as the second. It is written in the best Greek of the New Testament, in the style of an educated historian, and it is the Gospel with the most stories about outsiders: women, the poor, Samaritans, tax collectors and sinners.

The author is Luke, whom Paul calls his dear friend and physician (Colossians 4:14), and who traveled with Paul on some of his journeys. He was probably a Gentile, the only one to write a book of the New Testament. In the preface he says that he has investigated everything from the beginning and is writing an orderly account for Theophilus, so that he may know the certainty of what he was taught. It was probably written between AD 60 and 80.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 and 2: the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, with songs from Mary, Zechariah and Simeon.
- Chapters 3 to 9: baptism, temptation and ministry in Galilee.
- Chapters 9 to 19: the long journey to Jerusalem, which holds most of the material found only in Luke, such as the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep and coin, the prodigal son, and Zacchaeus.
- Chapters 19 to 24: Jerusalem, the crucifixion, the resurrection and the road to Emmaus.
## What to look for

Luke is the Gospel of the seeking God. The key verse is 19:10: "the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost." Watch for prayer, joy, the Holy Spirit, and the way Jesus lifts up the overlooked. The three parables in chapter 15 are the heart of it. Because Luke goes on to write Acts, he shows how the story of Jesus continues through his church.

Malachi has four chapters in English Bibles and three in Hebrew, and it closes the Old Testament. The name means "my messenger," and some have wondered whether it is a title rather than a name. It is a book of arguments, in which God makes a charge, the people ask "How?", and God answers.

The book is usually dated to about 450 to 430 BC, after the temple had been rebuilt and the walls of the city repaired, when the first enthusiasm of the return had faded. Priests were offering blemished animals, the people were withholding tithes, marriages were breaking down, and some wondered if serving God paid off.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1:1 to 5: God's love for Israel, which the people doubt.
- Chapter 1:6 to 2:9: charges against the priests for dishonoring God's name.
- Chapter 2:10 to 16: unfaithfulness in marriage.
- Chapter 2:17 to 3:5: where is the God of justice? The messenger will come.
- Chapter 3:6 to 4:6: the call to return, with tithes, and a final promise that Elijah will be sent before the great day.
## What to look for

Malachi is about a love that is taken for granted. God tells the people he has loved them, and they respond with doubt. The book builds toward the promise of a messenger who will prepare the way, and the New Testament identifies him with John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10). Then it stops, and the Old Testament closes on a note of waiting, with four centuries of silence ahead.

Matthew has twenty-eight chapters and opens the New Testament. It is the Gospel most clearly written to show that Jesus is the long-promised Messiah of Israel, and it is full of quotations from the Old Testament, which Matthew says were fulfilled in Jesus' birth, ministry and death.

Early church tradition says the author was Matthew, also called Levi, the tax collector whom Jesus called to follow him. Many scholars date the Gospel between about AD 70 and 90, after Mark, whose outline it follows and expands, while others place it earlier. Its audience seems to have been Jewish believers who knew the Scriptures well, and its Greek is polished and orderly.
## How it is arranged
Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five great discourses, each ending with a phrase such as "When Jesus had finished saying these things."

- Chapters 1 and 2: genealogy, birth, the visit of the wise men, and flight to Egypt.
- Chapters 3 and 4: baptism and temptation.
- Chapters 5 to 7: the Sermon on the Mount.
- Chapters 8 to 10: miracles and the sending out of the Twelve.
- Chapters 11 to 13: growing opposition, and parables of the kingdom.
- Chapters 14 to 20: travels, the church (chapter 18), and teaching on the way to Jerusalem.
- Chapters 21 to 25: the last week of teaching, ending with the Olivet discourse.
- Chapters 26 to 28: the arrest, trial, crucifixion and resurrection.
## What to look for

The genealogy puts Jesus in the line of Abraham and David, and the book answers the question of what the kingdom of heaven is like. It ends with a commission: "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me," and therefore, go and make disciples of all nations. The first words in the Gospel say Jesus is "Immanuel," God with us, and the last say that he is with us to the end of the age.

Micah has seven chapters. Its author, from the village of Moresheth in Judah, prophesied in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, in the later eighth century BC, so he was a contemporary of Isaiah. He spoke to Samaria and Jerusalem, and he was concerned for ordinary people, who were being squeezed by greedy landowners and corrupt leaders.

The name Micah means "who is like the LORD?", and the last chapter closes with a play on it: "Who is a God like You?" The book has the shape of three cycles, each beginning with "hear" and each moving from judgment to hope.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 3: charges against Samaria and Jerusalem, and against rulers who devour the people like meat.
- Chapters 4 and 5: the future kingdom, with nations coming to learn God's ways, and a ruler from Bethlehem.
- Chapters 6 and 7: a courtroom scene, the famous summary of what God requires, a lament and a closing hymn of forgiveness.
## What to look for

The great sentences are at 6:8, "to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God," and at 5:2, which names Bethlehem as the birthplace of the one who will rule Israel. The chief priests and scribes quote it when Herod asks where the Messiah would be born (Matthew 2:5-6). The book closes with a statement of astonishing forgiveness, in which God hurls all sins into the depths of the sea.

Mark has sixteen chapters and is the shortest Gospel and, by the view of most scholars, the earliest. It moves quickly, using the word "immediately" again and again, and it gives a large share of its length to the last week of Jesus' life. Mark's Jesus is a man of action, who is also the suffering Son of God.

The author, according to a very early tradition, was John Mark, the companion of Peter, who wrote down what Peter preached. Mark appears in Acts and in Paul's letters. Most date the Gospel to about AD 55 to 70, probably written for Gentile readers in Rome, who are often given explanations of Jewish customs and Aramaic words.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 8: Jesus' ministry in Galilee and the surrounding regions, with miracles, parables and growing opposition, and ending with Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ.
- Chapters 8 to 10: the road to Jerusalem, with three predictions of his death and teaching about discipleship.
- Chapters 11 to 16: Jerusalem, the last teaching, the cross and the empty tomb.
## What to look for

Mark keeps Jesus' identity half hidden. Demons recognize him and are told to be silent, and the disciples, who are slow to understand, only grasp it partway. At the midpoint Peter says, "You are the Christ," and Jesus at once begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer. The turning point is 10:45: "the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many." Note too that the earliest manuscripts end at 16:8, with the women fleeing in fear, and the longer ending appears in later copies.

Nahum has three chapters and is a poem about the fall of Nineveh. Its name means "comfort," and the comfort is for the people whom Assyria had crushed. More than a century after Jonah's preaching, when Nineveh's repentance had faded, Nahum announces its downfall.

The prophecy falls between the fall of the Egyptian city of Thebes to the Assyrians in 663 BC, which it mentions as a past event (3:8), and the fall of Nineveh to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC. It would be a mistake to read the book as only an outburst of nationalism. It is a statement that God sees brutality and will not let it stand.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: a hymn to God as a jealous, avenging and yet good God, who is a refuge for those who trust him.
- Chapter 2: a vivid description of the attack on the city.
- Chapter 3: the reasons for judgment, with bloodshed, deceit and plunder, and a closing taunt.
## What to look for

The book balances two truths: "The LORD is slow to anger and great in power; the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished," and "The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress." It is a word for people who suffer under cruel power, and it assures them that cruelty does not last forever. A line about the feet of one who brings good news (Nahum 1:15) is shared with Isaiah 52:7.

Numbers has thirty-six chapters. The English title, from the Greek, refers to the two censuses of Israel's men that open the book and begin its second half. The Hebrew name, Bemidbar, "In the wilderness," is closer to the story, which is about forty years of wandering between Sinai and the edge of the promised land.

Tradition names Moses as author. Its events fall in the years after the exodus, whether you date that to 1446 or 1260 BC. Some stories are told with plain frankness about the failures of Israel and also of Moses and Aaron.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 10: at Sinai. The census, the order of the camp, the work of the Levites, laws for purity, and the priestly blessing.
- Chapters 11 to 20: the journey and the rebellions. The spies at Kadesh, the refusal to enter the land, Korah's revolt, and Moses striking the rock.
- Chapters 21 to 25: the approach to Canaan, including the bronze serpent, Balaam and his donkey, and trouble with Moab.
- Chapters 26 to 36: the second census, the new generation, Joshua named as successor, and instructions for settling the land.
## What to look for

The theme is the contrast between God's faithfulness and Israel's unbelief. People grumble about food, water and leaders, and at Kadesh they refuse to trust God's promise, so an entire generation dies in the desert. Yet God keeps feeding them and does not cancel the plan. Even Balaam, hired to curse Israel, ends up blessing them. Paul uses the wilderness years as a warning for Christians (1 Corinthians 10), and Jesus uses the bronze serpent as a picture of his own cross.

Obadiah has one chapter of twenty-one verses and is the shortest book in the Old Testament. The name means "servant of the LORD," and there are a dozen men by that name in the Bible, so it is not clear which one wrote this. The book is a single oracle against Edom.

Edom, south of the Dead Sea, was the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother, and the two peoples had been enemies for centuries. The prophecy seems to be written after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom gloated, helped plunder the city and cut off those trying to escape (verses 10 to 14). Psalm 137:7 shows that Judah remembered this.
## How it is arranged

- Verses 1 to 9: Edom's pride, secure in its rock fortresses, will be brought down.
- Verses 10 to 14: the charge, that Edom stood aside and rejoiced when its brother was in trouble.
- Verses 15 to 21: the day of the LORD for all the nations, and the restoration of Israel, so that "the kingdom will belong to the LORD."
## What to look for

Obadiah teaches that pride and the failure to help a brother in trouble are sins that God judges. The measure is a fair one: "As you have done, it will be done to you." Its closing verse points beyond the local story to the rule of God over all. The book also reminds us how much family feeling runs through the Old Testament, starting with Jacob and Esau in Genesis.

Philemon is one chapter of twenty-five verses and is the shortest of Paul's letters, and the only one in the New Testament that is a purely personal note to a friend about a private matter. It is about a runaway slave and about how a Christian ought to think of him.

Philemon was a wealthy believer in Colossae, in whose home the church met. His slave Onesimus had run away, perhaps with some money, and had somehow met Paul in prison, probably in Rome around AD 60 to 62, and had become a Christian. Paul sends him back with this letter, carried together with the one to the Colossians.
## How it is arranged

- Verses 1 to 7: greeting and thanks for Philemon's love and faith.
- Verses 8 to 16: Paul's appeal for Onesimus, whom he calls his own child, and who is "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother."
- Verses 17 to 25: "receive him as you would receive me," with an offer to repay anything he owes, and a hope of visiting.
## What to look for

Paul is gentle and clever. He could command, but he appeals, and he uses the language of partnership and of family to ask Philemon to receive Onesimus. He does not say outright that slavery should end, but he sets a principle that undermines it, since two men are now brothers in Christ. Many readers have noticed the shape of the gospel here: one who owes a debt, and another who steps in and says, "charge it to my account."

Philippians has four chapters and is the warmest of Paul's letters, a thank-you note that turns into a lesson about joy. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia and the first city in Europe where Paul planted a church, on his second journey (Acts 16). The people there had supported him over the years and had just sent a gift by Epaphroditus.

Paul wrote from prison, most likely in Rome around AD 60 to 62, though Ephesus and Caesarea have been proposed. He did not know if he would be freed or executed, and yet the letter is full of joy and rejoicing. He writes to reassure them, to thank them and to urge them to stand together.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: thanksgiving, Paul's circumstances, and the call to live worthy of the gospel. "To live is Christ and to die is gain."
- Chapter 2: unity and humility, supported by the great hymn about Christ, who made himself nothing and was exalted. Timothy and Epaphroditus are commended.
- Chapter 3: a warning against those who trust in the flesh, and Paul's own testimony of counting everything as loss for the sake of knowing Christ.
- Chapter 4: appeals to unity and peace, "Rejoice in the Lord always," and thanks for the gift.
## What to look for

The word that keeps coming back is joy, though the writer is chained to a Roman guard. Paul has learned the secret of being content in plenty and in need, and the source is Christ. The hymn in chapter 2 is among the earliest Christian confessions and says that every knee will bow, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.

Proverbs has thirty-one chapters of short, memorable sayings, and it is the Bible's main book of wisdom. A proverb in the Bible is a pointed observation about how life usually works under God's rule. It is not a promise or a guarantee, and reading it that way is a common mistake.

Solomon is named at the start (1:1) and again at 10:1 and 25:1, where "the men of Hezekiah" are said to have copied more of his sayings about two centuries later. Two other voices appear, Agur in chapter 30 and King Lemuel in chapter 31. The book probably took its final form in the days of Hezekiah or later.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 9: a father urges his son to seek wisdom and avoid folly, with Wisdom and Folly pictured as two women calling from the street.
- Chapters 10 to 22: Solomon's sayings, mostly two-line contrasts.
- Chapters 22 to 24: sayings of the wise, including warnings and advice for rulers.
- Chapters 25 to 29: more of Solomon's proverbs, gathered under Hezekiah.
- Chapters 30 and 31: the words of Agur and Lemuel, and a closing poem on the woman of strength.
## What to look for

The foundation is in chapter 1: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." Wisdom is skill for living, and it begins in reverence. Look at topics such as speech, money, work, friendship, anger and family. Notice that proverbs often pair up and seem to contradict each other (see 26:4-5), because wisdom is knowing which saying fits which situation. In chapter 8 Wisdom speaks as one present at creation, and Paul says Christ is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24).
