The book of Psalms has 150 poems and is the longest book in the Bible, the hymnbook and prayer book of Israel. The Hebrew title is Tehillim, "Praises," although many of the psalms are laments. Jesus and the apostles quote it often, and Christians have prayed and sung it for two thousand years.

The psalms were written over perhaps a thousand years. The headings credit David with seventy-three, Asaph with twelve, the sons of Korah with eleven, and Solomon, Moses (Psalm 90), Ethan and Heman with a few. Many are anonymous. They were collected over time into five books, perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, and the whole was in place by the time of the second temple.
## How it is arranged

- Book 1, Psalms 1 to 41: mostly David's psalms, many of them laments and personal prayers.
- Book 2, Psalms 42 to 72: more of David, and the psalms of Korah, ending with a prayer for the king.
- Book 3, Psalms 73 to 89: Asaph and the psalms of national crisis.
- Book 4, Psalms 90 to 106: the LORD as King, in the wake of exile.
- Book 5, Psalms 107 to 150: thanksgiving, the Songs of Ascents (120 to 134), Psalm 119, and the closing praise.
## What to look for

Learn the kinds of psalm. Laments cry out of trouble and usually turn to trust. Hymns praise God for who he is. Thanksgiving psalms look back on rescue. Royal psalms, such as Psalms 2 and 110, point toward a king whom the New Testament identifies as Christ. Wisdom psalms, like Psalm 1, contrast two paths. The Psalms give honest words to every mood, and they teach that bringing a hard feeling to God is itself an act of faith.

Revelation has twenty-two chapters and is the last book of the Bible. Its first word in Greek is apokalypsis, "unveiling," which is why it is also called the Apocalypse. It is a letter, a prophecy and a vision, full of symbols drawn from Daniel, Ezekiel and the rest of the Old Testament. It is easy to misread and also one of the most hopeful books in Scripture.

The author calls himself John and says that he was on the island of Patmos "because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus." Tradition identifies him with the apostle. Most scholars date the book to about AD 95, under the emperor Domitian, when Christians were under pressure to join in the worship of Caesar. Some prefer the late 60s, soon after Nero.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: the vision of the risen Christ among seven lampstands.
- Chapters 2 and 3: seven letters to seven churches in Asia Minor.
- Chapters 4 and 5: the throne of God and the Lamb who was slain.
- Chapters 6 to 16: the seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls, with visions in between.
- Chapters 17 to 20: the fall of Babylon, the return of Christ, and the final judgment.
- Chapters 21 and 22: the new heaven and the new earth, and the new Jerusalem.
## How to read it

Christians have understood it in four main ways. Some see it as describing events of the first century. Some see it as a sweep of church history. Some see most of it as still future. Others see it as a set of timeless pictures of the conflict between Christ and evil. The book itself says it was written to encourage believers who were suffering: Christ is alive, he holds history in his hand, and he will win. The last prayer is the church's own: "Come, Lord Jesus."

Romans has sixteen chapters and is Paul's longest and most systematic letter. It is the clearest explanation in the New Testament of what the gospel is, and it has shaped Christian thought more than any other book, from Augustine through Luther and Wesley.

Paul wrote it from Corinth, probably in the winter of AD 56 to 57, near the end of his third journey. He had never visited Rome, where the church included both Jews and Gentiles, and he wanted their help for a mission to Spain. Because he was about to take a collection to Jerusalem, and because he did not know what awaited him, he set out his gospel carefully.
## How it is arranged

- 1:1 to 17: greeting, and the theme: the gospel is the power of God for salvation, and the righteous will live by faith.
- 1:18 to 3:20: the whole world, Gentile and Jew, is under sin.
- 3:21 to 5:21: God makes people right through faith in Christ, as with Abraham, and Adam and Christ are compared.
- Chapters 6 to 8: new life in the Spirit, freedom from sin and from condemnation.
- Chapters 9 to 11: God's faithfulness to Israel, and the place of Gentiles.
- 12:1 to 15:13: how to live, including love, government and welcoming those who disagree.
- 15:14 to 16:27: travel plans and greetings.
## What to look for

Follow the argument. Chapters 1 to 3 diagnose the problem, 3 to 5 give the remedy, and 6 to 8 describe a life lived in the Spirit. The result is "no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (8:1). Then Paul says that all this, from sin to glory, is mercy, and he breaks into praise at the end of chapter 11. Read the last chapters as the practical fruit of the earlier doctrine.

Ruth has four chapters and is a short story, almost a novella, of exceptional beauty. It is set "in the days when the judges ruled," which makes it a gleam of light against the dark background of Judges. In the Christian Old Testament it follows Judges. The Hebrew Bible places it among the Writings and reads it at the feast of Weeks.

The author is unnamed, though Jewish tradition says Samuel. The setting is the period of the judges, and the genealogy at the end, which reaches David, suggests it was written in or after his time. It was meant to be read as a quiet answer to the question of how God works in ordinary lives during hard years.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: famine, a move to Moab, three deaths, and the return of Naomi with Ruth.
- Chapter 2: Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz and finds his kindness.
- Chapter 3: Naomi's plan, and Ruth's request to Boaz on the threshing floor.
- Chapter 4: Boaz acts as kinsman-redeemer at the town gate, marries Ruth, and a son is born.
## What to look for

Look for the quiet providence in a story where God rarely acts openly. Look for loyalty, shown by Ruth to Naomi and by Boaz to Ruth. Above all, look for the redeemer. Boaz is a relative who buys back what was lost, and the Bible's longer story uses that picture for Christ. The last verses place a foreign woman in the family tree of David, and therefore in the family tree of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

The Song of Solomon has eight chapters, and it is a collection of love poems between a young woman and a man, with a chorus of friends. Its Hebrew title, Shir Hashirim, means "the Song of Songs," that is, the best of songs. It is the only book in the Bible devoted entirely to romantic love.

The title says "of Solomon," which could mean by, for, or about him. If Solomon wrote it, the date would be the tenth century BC. Many scholars think the poems were collected later. The setting is the countryside and the city, with gardens, vineyards, gazelles and spices, in language that is unusually frank and tender for ancient poetry.
## How it is arranged
The book is hard to outline because it is a series of lyrical scenes, but readers usually see a rough progress.

- Chapters 1 to 3: courtship, longing and the first meetings.
- Chapters 3 to 5: the wedding and its night, and a dream of loss.
- Chapters 5 to 8: reconciliation, deepening love, and the seal of love in the closing chapters.
## How to read it

Christians have read the Song in three main ways. Many in the early and medieval church took it as an allegory of Christ and his church, or of God and the soul. Others read it as literal poetry about marriage, which God made good. Some hold both: it celebrates human love, and that love points to a greater one. The great statement at the end, "love is as strong as death," holds either way, and the Song shows that desire and commitment belong together (8:6-7).

Titus has three chapters and is the shortest of the Pastoral Letters. Titus was a Gentile convert and a trusted coworker of Paul, who had served in the difficult church at Corinth, and who was now left on the island of Crete to put things in order. The letter is a brief charge for that task.

The traditional date is about AD 62 to 64, after Paul's first Roman imprisonment, for the same reasons as 1 Timothy, though many scholars question Paul's authorship. The island of Crete had a reputation for dishonesty, and Paul quotes one of its own poets on the subject (1:12).
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: appoint elders in every town, men of proven character who can teach sound doctrine and refute opposition.
- Chapter 2: how different groups in the church should live, and why. The grace of God has appeared, teaching us to say no to ungodliness.
- Chapter 3: how to live in society, as good citizens, and a summary of the gospel.
## What to look for

The letter links belief and behavior. Good doctrine produces good works, and "doing good" is mentioned again and again. The two summaries of the gospel in 2:11 to 14 and 3:4 to 7 are among the clearest in the New Testament, and they say that salvation comes from God's kindness and mercy and not from our righteous deeds, by the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit.

Zechariah has fourteen chapters and is the longest of the Minor Prophets, rich in imagery and in hope. The name means "the LORD remembers." Zechariah was a priest as well as a prophet, and he began prophesying in 520 BC, two months after Haggai.

The book falls into two parts. Chapters 1 to 8 are dated to 520 to 518 BC and are addressed to the people rebuilding the temple. Chapters 9 to 14 are undated and are about a coming king and the final day of the LORD. Some scholars think the second part was written by someone else at a later time, and others hold that both parts come from Zechariah.
## How it is arranged

- Chapters 1 to 6: eight visions given in one night, including horsemen, a measuring line, the high priest Joshua in clean clothes, a lampstand and flying scroll.
- Chapters 7 and 8: a question about fasting, and promises of a restored Jerusalem.
- Chapters 9 to 11: the coming king on a donkey, and the rejected shepherd.
- Chapters 12 to 14: the pierced one, the cleansing fountain and the final day, when the LORD will be king over all the earth.
## What to look for

Zechariah encourages: the work is done "not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit," says the LORD. After Haggai's call to rebuild, he looks beyond the temple to the king. The New Testament draws on these chapters in the Gospels' accounts of Palm Sunday, the thirty pieces of silver and the piercing, and Revelation uses the same visions.

Zephaniah has three chapters and is a short, sharp prophecy about the day of the LORD. The prophet's name means "the LORD hides" or "treasures," and he traces his own family back four generations to a Hezekiah, perhaps the king, which would make him a royal descendant.

He prophesied in the days of Josiah, between about 640 and 609 BC, before or during Josiah's reforms. The mood is one of fear: Judah has lived through the long, wicked reign of Manasseh, and judgment seems close. The book was probably given early in Josiah's reign, before the great reform of 621 BC.
## How it is arranged

- Chapter 1: the day of the LORD, which will sweep away idolatry and the complacent.
- Chapter 2: a call to seek the LORD, and judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush and Assyria.
- Chapter 3: judgment on Jerusalem, followed by a promise of a purified remnant and a song of rejoicing.
## What to look for

The day of the LORD is a day of darkness, but those who seek him may be hidden. At the end comes one of the most surprising verses in the prophets: the LORD is in your midst, "He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing." God is not only the judge. He is the one who rejoices over his people and sings.
